amendment_status: Current Criminal Law (Came into force on 1st July 2024; repealed and replaced the Indian Penal Code, 1860).
content: Short title, extent and commencement: (1) This Act may be called the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. (2) It extends to the whole of India. (3) It came into force on the 1st day of July, 2024. Historical Status: Replaces the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (Act No. 45 of 1860). Offences committed on or after 1 July 2024 are prosecuted under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, while offences committed prior to 1 July 2024 continue to be governed by the Indian Penal Code, 1860.

amendment_status: Replaces IPC Sections 405/406 (Criminal Breach of Trust) and Section 420 (Cheating)
content: Criminal Breach of Trust and Cheating under BNS: Section 316 defines Criminal Breach of Trust: Whoever, being in any manner entrusted with property, dishonestly misappropriates or converts to his own use that property, commits criminal breach of trust. Section 318 defines Cheating: Whoever, by deceiving any person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person so deceived to deliver any property, commits cheating. Note: Section 318 of BNS corresponds to Section 420 of the repealed Indian Penal Code (IPC). Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property is punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.

Theft under BNS Section 303: Whoever, intending to take dishonestly any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent, moves that property in order to such taking, is said to commit theft. Punishment under Section 303(2): Whoever commits theft shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. In cases of theft of property valued under Rs. 5,000 where the offender is a first-time offender, community service may be ordered. This replaces Section 379 of IPC.

statute_name: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Act No. 46 of 2023)
amendment_status: Replaces Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC)
content: Information in cognizable cases (First Information Report / FIR): Every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence may be given orally or by electronic communication (Zero FIR / e-FIR) to an officer in charge of a police station. Section 173(1) allows information to be given irrespective of the area where the crime was committed (Zero FIR). When information is given electronically, it must be signed within three days by the person giving it. Preliminary enquiry may be conducted within 14 days in cases punishable between 3 to 7 years to assess prima facie case.

amendment_status: Corresponds to Section 438 of the repealed CrPC, 1973
content: Direction for grant of bail to person apprehending arrest (Anticipatory Bail): Where any person has reason to believe that he may be arrested on accusation of having committed a non-bailable offence, he may apply to the High Court or the Court of Session for a direction under this section; and that Court may, if it thinks fit, direct that in the event of such arrest, he shall be released on bail. The Court considers factors including the nature and gravity of accusation, criminal antecedents, and likelihood of fleeing from justice.

amendment_status: Replaces Section 65B of the repealed Indian Evidence Act, 1872
content: Admissibility of electronic or digital records: Section 61 provides that nothing in this Adhiniyam shall apply to deny admissibility of electronic or digital records in evidence on the ground that it is an electronic record. Section 63 governs the conditions for admissibility of electronic records (corresponding to old Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872). Any information contained in an electronic record produced by computer/device shall be deemed to be a document if certified by person in charge or owner in the specified Schedule form.

Consumer Rights and Remedies under CPA 2019: Defines 'consumer' as any person who buys goods or hires services for consideration, excluding commercial resale. Recognizes six consumer rights: right to be protected, right to be informed, right to be assured, right to be heard, right to seek redressal, and right to consumer awareness. Establishes three-tier redressal: District Commission (claims up to Rs. 50 Lakhs / revised jurisdiction), State Commission (claims Rs. 50 Lakhs to Rs. 2 Crores), and National Commission (claims exceeding Rs. 2 Crores). Section 35 provides procedure for filing complaint directly or through e-Daakhil portal.

Cybercrime, Identity Theft, and Cheating by Personation: Section 43 prescribes compensation for damage to computer systems, data theft, and unauthorized copying. Section 66C punishes identity theft (fraudulent use of electronic signature, password, or unique identification feature) with imprisonment up to 3 years and fine up to Rs. 1 Lakh. Section 66D punishes cheating by personation by using computer resources with imprisonment up to 3 years and fine up to Rs. 1 Lakh. Cybercrime complaints can be lodged on national cybercrime portal cybercrime.gov.in or helpline 1930.

amendment_status: Current fundamental contract law in India
content: Essential elements of valid contract and breach remedies: Section 10 provides that all agreements are contracts if they are made by free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object. Section 23 voids agreements where consideration or object is forbidden by law. Section 73 provides compensation for loss or damage caused by breach of contract: the injured party is entitled to receive compensation for direct, natural loss arising from the breach. Section 74 governs liquidated damages and penalties.

statute_name: Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (Act No. 4 of 1882)
amendment_status: Substantive property and tenancy law; read with State Rent Control Acts
content: Lease of Immovable Property and Rental Agreements: Section 105 defines a lease as a transfer of a right to enjoy property for a certain time or in perpetuity in consideration of a price or rent. Section 106 governs duration of leases in absence of written contract: leases for agricultural or manufacturing purposes require 6 months notice; leases for other purposes (residential/commercial) require 15 days notice expiring with the end of a tenancy month. Section 107 mandates that leases for more than one year must be registered by a registered instrument. State Model Tenancy Acts / Rent Control Acts also govern security deposits and eviction grounds.

statute_name: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (Act No. 22 of 2023)
content: Data Privacy and Data Principal Rights in India: Section 4 provides that personal data may only be processed for lawful purpose for which consent has been given, or for legitimate uses. Section 6 specifies requirements of valid consent: free, specific, informed, unconditional, and unambiguous. Data principals have rights to access information, correction and erasure of personal data, grievance redressal, and right to nominate. Significant Data Fiduciaries must appoint a Data Protection Officer based in India.

document_title: Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 / Labour Law Framework
statute_name: Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 & Code on Wages, 2019
amendment_status: Governs retrenchment and termination of workmen; to be consolidated into Occupational Safety & Social Security Codes
content: Employment Termination and Notice Requirements: Section 25F of Industrial Disputes Act mandates conditions precedent to retrenchment of workmen: one month notice in writing indicating reasons for retrenchment, or wages in lieu of notice, and retrenchment compensation equivalent to fifteen days average pay for every completed year of continuous service. For non-workman employees, terms of employment contract / offer letter and state Shops & Commercial Establishments Acts govern notice periods (typically 30 to 90 days) and severance pay.
